Core Tenant Security

Chapter 1What Core Tenant Security is

A SharePoint Framework web part that turns the Microsoft Entra sign-in log into a suite of purpose-built visualisations — so a tenant admin can spot impossible-travel events, conditional-access gaps, risky users, and brute-force attempts at a glance, and act on them, without leaving SharePoint.
Langate · Microsoft 365 Security
Overview
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Overview

The core views

Live globe

World map (flat or 3-D) with sign-in bubbles, impossible-travel arcs, a day/night overlay, and a 90-day time scrubber.

Conditional-Access Sankey

Flow diagram from all sign-ins → policies → outcomes, exposing gaps in policy coverage.

Per-user activity heatmap

A daily-volume calendar plus a weekday × hour grid coloured by sign-in count, Monday-first.

User-baseline diff cards

Each user’s usual countries, devices, apps and active hours, so anomalies stand out against their normal.

Brute-force / spray clusters

Failed sign-ins grouped by source IP, with a red banner when a spray actually succeeded.

Legacy-auth radar

Per-protocol breakdown of legacy authentication still in use — the highest-leverage thing to switch off.

Core Tenant Security · Overview
Langate  ·  7
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Overview · cont.

…and five more

Beyond the six analytical views above, the dashboard carries five action-oriented tabs — the places where an admin actually responds to what the charts surface:

  • Timeline — one person’s every sign-in and Defender event on a single chronological rail (Chapter 5).
  • Risk — the users Entra Identity Protection flagged, with one-click sign-out, whitelist, and write-back actions (Chapter 3).
  • Incidents and Alerts — Microsoft Defender XDR incidents and alerts mirrored into shared SharePoint lists for team triage (Chapter 4).
  • Audit — an append-only log of every in-tool action: who signed whom out, who whitelisted whom, and every triage edit.

How it gets the data

The web part runs entirely in the signed-in admin’s browser. It pulls /auditLogs/signIns from Microsoft Graph as a delegated call, dedupes and folds the events into daily aggregates and per-user baselines, and persists everything to a browser IndexedDB cache (cts-cache) with a 90-day rolling retention. On the next visit the dashboard warm-loads from that cache and paints immediately, while a background sync refreshes silently.

Who it's for

Core Tenant Security is built for three people who rarely have time to read a flat sign-in table. Every feature in this book is aimed at one of them — and most are useful to all three.

MSP / tenant admin

"Is anything wrong across my tenants this week?"

  • Globe & impossible-travel arcs
  • Conditional-Access gaps
  • Legacy-auth radar
Security analyst

"This account looks off — what happened, and what do I do?"

  • Risk panel + write-back
  • Per-user Timeline
  • Defender Incidents
First-line helpdesk

"A ticket landed — in plain words, is this bad?"

  • My Queue on Incidents
  • Plain-language triage
  • One-click sign-out

Overview · cont.

Filters and tabs

The filter strip at the top of the dashboard scopes most views to a date range, a list of picked users, and/or a list of picked Entra groups. Applying a filter does not issue a fresh Graph pull — the cache already holds the full retained window, so filtering is a fast, in-memory narrowing of the cached events. The only live Graph call a filter ever makes is resolving a picked group’s membership; a date-only or user-only filter makes none.

Five tabs are deliberately tenant-wide and ignore the filter — Risk, Brute Force, Incidents, Alerts, and Audit. Hiding a risky user or a spray pattern behind a filter is exactly the kind of thing a security admin must not have to think about, so when one of those tabs is active the filter inputs are dimmed and a one-line note explains why.

Baseline dims the date inputs only: each user’s “normal” is computed against their whole retained window, so a narrower date filter would invalidate the comparison. The user/group picker stays live on Baseline so you can still focus on the people you care about.

Every input takes effect on the gesture itself — picking a date, clicking a user in the dropdown, or clicking × on a chip applies immediately, with no separate Apply button. Clear wipes every filter at once, and Load example data swaps in a rich synthetic tenant so you can explore every view without a live sync.

Why this exists

The Entra portal’s built-in sign-in log is a flat table. For an MSP or internal admin running periodic reviews, the question is rarely "what was sign-in #4732?" — it’s "where are users coming from this week, who’s drifted from their normal pattern, which sprays landed, and what isn’t a Conditional Access policy covering?" Core Tenant Security answers those questions at a glance, and puts the response action one click away, in the same SharePoint page where the rest of the admin’s tools already live.

Analytics views · Conditional Access

Conditional-Access Sankey

A flow diagram that follows every sign-in left-to-right: all sign-ins → CA evaluated / no CA policy → passed / blocked. The width of each band is its volume, so the eye goes straight to the thickest flow — which is exactly where coverage either holds or leaks.

Healthy

Almost everything flows through "CA evaluated", and "Blocked by CA" is a thin but non-zero band — policies are both present and biting.

Red flag

A thick "No CA policy" band — those sign-ins were never evaluated. Click it to see which apps and users are slipping past your policies.

Core Tenant Security · Analytics views

Analytics views · Heatmap

Activity heatmap

Two grids: a daily-volume calendar (one cell per day, darker = busier) and an hour-of-day × day-of-week matrix, Monday-first, in your local time. Together they show a tenant’s working rhythm — and anything that happens outside it.

Healthy

A clean rectangle of activity through weekday office hours, fading on evenings and weekends — people working when you'd expect.

Red flag

Bright cells at 3 a.m. or across the weekend. Click the cell to see whose sign-ins lit it up — automation, or something worth a look.

Analytics views · Baselines

User baselines

One card per user, summarising their normal: the countries they sign in from, the operating systems and apps they use, and their active hours. It is the reference the Timeline’s anomaly tags are measured against — here you can see the whole roster’s normal at once.

Healthy

Tight, consistent cards — one or two countries, a known set of devices, predictable hours. This is what "normal" should look like.

Red flag

A card that suddenly lists a new country or an unfamiliar OS. Open the user's Timeline (Chapter 5) to see exactly when the pattern changed.

Analytics views · Baselines

MFA tokens & their lifespan

Every card carries an MFA badge showing how many multi-factor methods that person is currently using — the Microsoft Authenticator app, passkeys (FIDO2 security keys), Windows Hello, phone, email, and OATH tokens. The badge is colour-coded so weak coverage stands out at a glance: green for two or more active methods, amber for a single method, and red for none. An expired credential (such as an old Temporary Access Pass) is not counted — it is not something the user can sign in with today.

Click the MFA badge to open the full Authentication methods window. It opens with the person’s photo and a posture badge — Strong, Good, Weak, and so on — with a one-line reason (“a phishing-resistant method is registered”, “SMS/phone only”) and a short tally underneath (“4 phishing-resistant · 1 push · 2 weak”). The methods are then grouped by strength: Phishing-resistant (passkeys, Windows Hello), Good (the Authenticator app), Weak / phishable (SMS, email, OATH codes), and Inactive (anything expired, kept for the record but not counted). Each method shows its own icon, a strength tag, what it is (device name, phone number, or email — a personal email such as a hotmail address is flagged in amber, because it is a recovery door outside the organisation’s control), and how long ago it was registered (“2 years ago”). Where a person has several of the same kind — four Windows Hello devices, say — they fold into one row you can expand. A live Temporary Access Pass shows a countdown; an expired one sits in Inactive. At the foot, Manage authentication methods and Open in Entra portal jump to the Entra portal, where an administrator can reset or revoke a method.

Each active method also shows whether it is actually being used to sign in. The dashboard cross-references every registered method against the last 90 days of sign-in logs (which record the method each sign-in used): a method that has signed in recently reads “Used 3 days ago”, while one that never appears is flagged in amber — “Not used to sign in in the last N days” — with a summary line at the top counting how many registered methods are going unused. That surfaces stale credentials: a Windows Hello or passkey registered years ago that the person has quietly stopped using is a method worth removing (every extra registered method is one more thing an attacker could try to take over). “Not used” here means no interactive sign-in used it in the window — a method last used to establish a long-lived session, then only silently refreshed since, will correctly read as unused.

What to look for. A red or amber badge is a user one lost phone away from being locked out — or, if an attacker registers a fresh token, a brand-new method dated “registered today” on an account that has had the same passkey for years. A live Temporary Access Pass that nobody expected is worth a second look too.

One-time setup. Reading a user’s registered methods needs the UserAuthenticationMethod.Read.All Graph permission. A global administrator grants it once, in SharePoint Admin Center → Advanced → API access; until then the badge reads “MFA · n/a”.

Analytics views · Brute force

Brute-force & spray clusters

Failed sign-ins grouped by source IP and drawn as bubbles — bigger and redder means more failures — with a ranked "top source IPs" list beside them. It turns a wall of failure events into a handful of obvious offenders.

Spray that succeeded. If one IP failed against many accounts and then logged one of them in, a red banner appears at the top of this tab — the strongest "breached now" signal the tool produces. Each named account links straight to its Timeline.

Core Tenant Security · Analytics views
Langate  ·  18
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Analytics views · Legacy auth

Legacy-auth radar

Legacy authentication protocols (basic auth, authenticated SMTP, older clients) can’t do MFA, so they are the single most-exploited door in a tenant. The radar breaks down what is still in use by protocol, with KPI tiles for the last 24 hours, the 90-day total, the number of protocols seen, and how many days had any legacy auth.

Highest-leverage fix. A non-zero radar is a to-do list: each spoke is a protocol you can move to block with a Conditional-Access policy. Drive it to zero and you've closed the easiest path an attacker has.

Next Steps

Chapter 2Next steps

The first release covers Microsoft Entra sign-in activity end-to-end. The roadmap below captures parallel data sources that would complement that picture — starting with the network layer.

Integrate Ubiquiti / UniFi telemetry Planned

Ubiquiti’s UniFi platform exposes several APIs that pair well with the Entra view. Where Entra answers "who signed in from where," UniFi answers "what device, on which switch port, behind which firewall rule." Together they close the gap between identity events and network events.

Which API to use

API Hosting What it’s good for
UniFi Site Manager Cloud
api.ui.com		 Cloud, API key Fleet inventory and health across many sites. Read-mostly. Light on per-client security telemetry. Easy to authenticate.
UniFi Network Controller
/proxy/network/api		 Local controller or UniFi OS device The data goldmine for this use case. Events, IDS/IPS alarms, historical sessions, DPI per client, firewall config. Officially undocumented but well-mapped by the community.
UniFi Protect UniFi OS device Cameras, motion events, doorbell. Adjacent to physical-security correlation but out of scope for v1.
UISP UISP server, token auth ISP / WISP equipment. Only relevant if Langate ever monitors customer-edge gear directly.

Next Steps

What we would surface in the dashboard

  • Identity × network correlation: when a risky Entra sign-in happens, show which UniFi client matched the source IP and what app categories it’s been using (from DPI).
  • IDS/IPS overlay on the globe: the existing globe view already plots Entra dots by country; UniFi stat/alarm hits can render alongside, in red.
  • Session-history join: UniFi stat/sessions gives a per-client byte-and-duration log — a natural anomaly signal for the baseline view.
  • Firewall-rule lineage: reading rest/firewallrule lets the doc generate an up-to-date diagram of egress and inter-VLAN policy without screenshotting the UniFi UI.

Langate  ·  21

Next Steps

Build plan

  1. Decide auth boundary — the controller API needs a session cookie from a local controller, so a small shared proxy (Azure Function or container) is likely needed to keep credentials out of the browser. Site Manager Cloud is the opposite: an API key works directly from the SPFx web part via a CORS-friendly fetch.
  2. Add a UniFiClient alongside GraphSignInClient in the SPFx project, mirroring the same retry / paging / chunking pattern already used for Graph.
  3. Store UniFi credentials per-admin in the same private OneDrive store the Entra data uses — one consistent secret-handling story.
  4. Add a seventh dashboard view ("Network") through the existing AggregateViewCtor dispatch — one ctor-reference line, no new boilerplate in the web part.
Why this is a "next step" and not v1: Entra alone already answers the most-asked questions, and Ubiquiti coverage is uneven across Langate customers. We add it when a customer with UniFi gear requests it, not speculatively.

Other parallel data sources Under consideration

The same integration pattern — per-admin credentials, retry-aware client, OneDrive-cached aggregates, one new view — could fold in any of the following without re-architecting the web part:

  • Microsoft Defender for Identity alerts
  • Microsoft Defender for Endpoint device-risk scores
  • Exchange Online message-trace logs (mail-flow anomalies)
  • Azure Activity Log (admin-action audit beyond sign-ins)

None of these are committed work — the Ubiquiti integration is the first concrete next step.

Chapter 3The Risk Panel

The users Entra Identity Protection has flagged as risky — one card per user, near-identical attempts collapsed to a single line — with one-click force sign-out, a shared whitelist, and write-back actions that close the case in Entra.

Risk Panel
Core Tenant Security · Risk Panel
Langate  ·  24
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Risk Panel

Two surfaces, one set of data

Header badge → drawer

A red, pulsing Risk N pill sits in the dashboard header and is visible from every tab. Clicking it slides a drawer in from the right with the full risk content.

Dedicated Risk tab

The tab strip carries a Risk tab between Baseline and Brute Force. It paints the same two sections as the drawer, full-width, with its own scroll — useful when you want the risk view as the primary surface.

What the panel shows

Two sections, in order:

  1. Risky users — one expandable card per user, deduplicated across the loaded window, highest score first. The section heading shows the user count and the total risky sign-ins behind them ("Risky users (2) · 17 sign-ins").
  2. Whitelisted — the current contents of the trusted-users list. Each row carries a Remove button.

Grouped sign-ins — one card per user

Each user card carries the person's identity (photo, name and sign-in name), the risk badge, a roll-up summary line ("14 risky sign-ins · 1 location · last …"), and a single set of actions. Below the header, that user's risky sign-ins are folded into groups — sign-ins that share the same location (city + country) and service collapse into one row.

The ×N count pill

Each group shows how many sign-ins it folds. A password-spray burst of 14 identical attempts becomes a single ×14 row instead of 14 separate lines, with the time span (first → last) underneath.

Expand for the detail

A group with more than one sign-in expands on click to list the individual attempts (time and IP). The group row also shows the IP summary ("2 IPs"), the service used, and colour-coded reason chips (red for malicious / spray / leaked, gold for other anomalies).

The Sign-out, Whitelist and Timeline actions live once on each user card — not on every sign-in as in the previous flat list — so acting on a noisy account is a single click rather than a hunt through repeated rows.

Langate · Core Tenant Security
Risk Panel

Risk level (the coloured badge)

Each row carries a badge that mirrors the Entra Identity Protection level. The colour scheme:

  • NONE (grey) — no elevated risk.
  • LOW (gold) — Entra flagged but not actionable on its own.
  • MED (red tint) — medium risk; worth a look.
  • HIGH (solid red) — high risk or confirmed compromise; act now.

A row is shown only when the level is medium / high or the risk state is atRisk / confirmedCompromised. On lower licence tiers (anything below Entra ID P2) the risk fields stay blank, so the badge count will read Risk 0.

Force sign-out

Every user row has a red Sign out button. Clicking it opens a confirmation dialog (you can always cancel), and on confirm posts to Microsoft Graph POST /users/{id}/revokeSignInSessions. Entra invalidates every refresh token Entra has issued for the user, forcing them to re-authenticate on every app and device.

Token revocation propagates to all resource providers within about 10 minutes. Access tokens already in flight may continue to work for up to an hour until they expire. The drawer's top hint repeats this so admins don't assume the click failed when they see a brief grace period.

The whitelist

Whitelisted users are skipped by both the badge count and the risk lists — useful for service accounts, intentionally legacy-auth applications, or any account the team has already reviewed and cleared.

  • The whitelist lives in a SharePoint list named CTS Trusted Users on the current site (internal name CtsTrustedUsers).
  • The list inherits the site's permissions — every admin who can see the dashboard can read and edit it.
  • The list is provisioned automatically on first use; you do not need to create it manually.

To add a user, click Whitelist on any risk row. A small dialog opens that lets you type an optional Reason — this gets stored on the list item so the next admin who looks understands why the account is trusted. Click Remove on a whitelist row to put the account back into risk detection.

The dashboard polls the list every 5 minutes so adds and removes by other admins show up without a page reload.

Langate · Core Tenant Security
Risk Panel · Write-back actions

Write-back: closing the loop in Entra

Sign-out ends the current sessions, but it does not change how Entra thinks about the account. Three further buttons on each risk card write the verdict straight back to Microsoft Entra Identity Protection — so the dashboard isn’t just a viewer, it’s where the case gets closed. Each one confirms first, then records the action to the Audit log.

Confirm compromised

Tells Entra the account really is taken over (riskyUsers/confirmCompromised), raising its risk to high and feeding the signal back into Identity Protection.

Dismiss risk

Clears a false positive (riskyUsers/dismiss) so a known-good user stops cluttering the list — the considered alternative to whitelisting.

Disable account goes further still: it sets accountEnabled = false via PATCH /users/{id}, blocking every future sign-in until an admin re-enables the user. It is the heaviest hammer on the card, so it always asks for confirmation first.

Every action is logged

Force sign-out, whitelist add/remove, and all three write-backs are recorded to an append-only SharePoint list, CTS Action Log, surfaced on the Audit tab. Each row stamps who acted, what they did, which account it targeted, when, and the outcome — so a team can answer "who signed this user out, and why?" without guessing.

The audit write is deliberately soft-fail: if logging an action ever fails, the action itself still goes through and the dashboard stays up — a security tool must never refuse to sign out an attacker because a list write hiccuped. A failed log row is flagged rather than silently dropped.

Langate · Core Tenant Security
Risk Panel

First-deploy checklist

The risk panel needs these Microsoft Graph permissions, which an admin must approve once per tenant:

  1. Open SharePoint Admin Center.
  2. Go to Advanced → API access.
  3. Find the pending requests filed by the Core Tenant Security web part and click Approve for each:
    • User.RevokeSessions.All — required for the Sign-out button.
    • Sites.Manage.All — required so the web part can auto-provision the CTS Trusted Users and CTS Action Log lists on first run.
    • IdentityRiskyUser.ReadWrite.All — required for Confirm compromised / Dismiss risk.
    • User.EnableDisableAccount.All — required for Disable account.

Approvals propagate within a minute or two. Until they are approved, the Sign-out button surfaces a clear error modal and the Whitelist button fails noisily — refresh the page after approval and both will start working.

If the panel is empty

  • Badge reads "Risk 0": no Entra-flagged risky users in the loaded window. On non-P2 tenants this is the expected steady-state.
  • Whitelist section says "No users are currently whitelisted": the SP list exists but is empty — normal on first deploy.
  • Sign-out failed modal: the User.RevokeSessions.All permission has not been granted yet (see checklist above).

Chapter 4The Incidents tab

Microsoft Defender XDR incidents mirrored into a shared SharePoint list every admin can see and triage from inside the dashboard. Status, assignee and notes survive every refresh and are visible to the whole team — no per-user copy, no fork.
Langate · Microsoft 365 Security
Incidents
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Incidents

Two surfaces, one source of truth

The dashboard tab

The seventh tab in the tab strip carries one row per incident. Each row shows severity, name, age, alert count, Defender status, and the admin-owned Local status badge. Click Triage to open an inline editor below the row.

The SharePoint list

The list CTS Incidents on the current site is the source of truth. Every triage edit lands there first, then re-renders the dashboard. You can also open the list directly in SharePoint to filter, sort, set up alerts on, or export.

What each row shows

  • Severity pill — HIGH / MED / LOW / INFO, colour-coded. Inherited from Defender; updated on every sync.
  • Display name — the incident's title in Defender. Click Details for the full alert breakdown + a deep link to Defender XDR.
  • Last update — the incident's lastUpdateDateTime, in your browser's local timezone.
  • Alerts · N — how many individual alerts roll up under this incident.
  • Defender status — the upstream status (active / inProgress / resolved / redirected). Refreshed on every sync.
  • Local status badge — New, Investigating, Mitigated, or Closed. This is what you control.
  • Local assignee — whichever admin on your team owns the incident this week.
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Incidents · My Queue

My Queue — just my work

A segmented control at the top of the tab cuts the full list down to what one person needs to act on:

  • All — every incident.
  • Assigned to me (N) — only the incidents whose Local assignee matches the signed-in admin.
  • Unassigned (N) — incidents nobody has picked up yet, so they don’t fall through the cracks.

Plain language, not jargon

Defender describes incidents in its own vocabulary. Each row adds two human sentences a first-line helpdesk worker can act on without a security background — a "what this means" summary and a "do this next" suggestion — plus an age badge so a stale incident is obvious at a glance.

Langate · Core Tenant Security
Incidents · Triage workflow

Triaging an incident

  1. Click the green Triage button on the row.
  2. An inline editor expands below the row with three controls:
    • Status dropdown — pick one of New, Investigating, Mitigated, Closed.
    • Assignee text field — type a name or email; this is plain text, not a people picker, so service accounts and external addresses are welcome.
    • Notes multi-line text — visible to every dashboard admin. Use it to log what you saw, what you did, and what you're waiting on.
  3. Click Save. The row repaints with the new status badge; the change is written back to the SharePoint list.
  4. Click Cancel to drop the edits without saving.

A re-sync from Defender will refresh the severity, Defender status, alert roll-up, and any classification / determination you may have set in the Defender portal — it will NOT touch the Local Status, Local Assignee, or Local Notes. Your triage state survives every sync.

Triaging an individual alert

Defender groups related alerts under one incident. For some investigations you need triage state on the alerts themselves (one analyst working the lateral-movement alert, another working the brute-force alert under the same parent incident). The Incidents tab supports this:

  1. Open the incident's Triage editor as above.
  2. Scroll past the incident-level controls to the Alerts sub-section. Each alert is a row with its own severity pill, title, category, detection source, and a Local-status badge.
  3. Click Triage alert on any alert row. A nested editor opens with its own Status / Assignee / Notes controls, scoped to that single alert.
  4. Click Save. The alert's badge updates and the change is persisted to a separate SharePoint list CTS Alert Triage.

Per-alert triage lives in its own list so individual alerts can be searched, filtered, and reported on independently of their parent incident — useful when one alert recurs across many incidents and you want to track it as a workstream of its own. The Defender-side alert state stays in the incident row's AlertsJson column, so you never lose the upstream view.

Langate · Core Tenant Security
Incidents · Setup & troubleshooting

What the dashboard does in the background

  • On every page load, the web part pulls Defender incidents updated in the last 90 days via Microsoft Graph. Existing rows in CTS Incidents are PATCHed with the fresh Defender mirror; new ids land as new rows with LocalStatus = "New".
  • The sync runs in parallel with the sign-in sync, so the dashboard doesn't wait on Defender.
  • Tenants without a Defender XDR license get a clean "Defender XDR is not licensed" note instead of an error.

First-deploy checklist

Two extra Microsoft Graph permissions are needed for the Incidents tab. An admin must approve them once per tenant:

  1. Open SharePoint Admin Center.
  2. Go to Advanced → API access.
  3. Find the two new pending requests filed by Core Tenant Security and click Approve for each:
    • SecurityIncident.Read.All
    • SecurityAlert.Read.All
  4. The signed-in admin also needs at least the Security Reader Entra role.
  5. The two SharePoint lists (CTS Incidents and CTS Alert Triage) are provisioned automatically on the first sync.

Until the two scopes are approved the tab paints empty with a "Defender XDR is not licensed on this tenant" hint — even on tenants that do have the license. Refresh the page after approval and the first sync populates the list.

If the tab is empty

  • "Defender XDR is not licensed on this tenant": Graph returned 403. Usually the permission grant above is still pending; otherwise the tenant genuinely doesn't have the license.
  • "No Defender incidents in the loaded window": the Graph call worked but no incidents were updated in the last 90 days — not a regression, just a quiet tenant.
  • Triage save modal: the Sites.Manage.All permission has not been granted, or one of the two CTS lists was deleted out from under the dashboard. The dashboard recreates the lists on its next sync; refresh after that runs.

Choosing who to look at

Search any user

The people-picker at the top searches your whole tenant by name or email. Type a few letters, click a match, and their timeline builds instantly.

Quick-pick chips

Two ready-made shortlists sit next to the search box: At risk (everyone with a risky sign-in in the window, riskiest first) and Most active (the busiest accounts). One click loads that user.

Timeline · The rail

What the rail shows

Every event is a card on a vertical rail, with a colour-coded dot marking its type:

  • Green — a successful sign-in.
  • Amber — a failed sign-in.
  • Red — a risky sign-in (flagged by Entra Identity Protection).
  • Purple — a Defender alert naming this user.
  • Pink — a Defender incident naming this user.
  • Teal — a directory change (“what changed”) that this user either made or was the subject of — a role grant, an app consent, a password reset, an MFA-method registration, a Conditional-Access edit, or a group change.

Each card carries the local time, what happened, where from (city + country), the device (with an OS icon and the raw user-agent on hover), the app, the Conditional Access result, and any risk reasons. Click a card to open its full detail, including a deep link to the Entra sign-in logs or the Microsoft Defender portal.

Core Tenant Security · Timeline
Langate  ·  36
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Timeline · Reading the signals

Anomaly tags — what's out of the ordinary

The dashboard already learns each user's normal pattern (their Baseline). On the timeline, any sign-in that breaks that pattern gets a gold tag so it stands out at a glance:

  • New country — a sign-in from a country this user is not normally seen in.
  • New device — an operating system that isn't part of their usual kit.
  • New app — an application they don't normally use.
  • Off-hours — a sign-in outside their usual active hours.

A single tag is rarely cause for alarm — people travel and buy new phones. But a cluster (new country and new device and off-hours, all on the same risky sign-in) is the classic shape of an account takeover, and the timeline puts that shape right in front of you.

The stats ribbon and mini-map

Above the rail, a row of tiles summarises the window for this user: sign-ins, failures, risky sign-ins, distinct countries, distinct devices, and Defender alert / incident counts. Below it, a density mini-map shows one bar per day — taller bars are busier days, and red bars mark days that contained a risky sign-in or a Defender event. Click any bar to jump straight to that day on the rail.

Core Tenant Security · Timeline
Langate  ·  37
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Timeline · Reading the signals

Focusing the view

The filter toggles narrow the rail without losing the big picture (the stats and mini-map always reflect everything):

  • All — everything, merged.
  • Sign-ins — only sign-in activity (success, failure, risky).
  • Risky — only the risky sign-ins.
  • Defender — only the Defender alerts and incidents.
  • Directory — only the directory changes (“what changed”) that involve this user.

Two more shortcuts make a long history quick to work: the stat tiles are clickable — tap "Risky" or "Failed" and the rail filters to just those — and a search box matches across title, location, IP, device, app, and anomaly tags, so you can pull every sign-in from one IP in a keystroke.

Where the data comes from

The timeline reuses data the dashboard has already gathered — there is no extra permission to approve and nothing new to switch on. Sign-ins come from the same 90-day cache the rest of the dashboard uses; the Defender overlay reuses the Incidents/Alerts feed and links an alert to a user through the user accounts named in the alert's evidence. If a tenant has no Defender license, the timeline simply shows the sign-in history with no purple or pink cards.

Core Tenant Security · Timeline
Langate  ·  38
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Timeline · What changed

Directory changes — the “what changed” lane

Sign-ins answer who got in. They don't answer the equally important question an investigator asks next: what was changed in the directory — and by whom? The teal cards on the rail close that gap. Alongside this user's sign-ins and Defender events, the timeline now overlays the administrative changes that touch them, drawn from the Entra audit log:

  • Role grants — the user was added to (or removed from) a directory role such as Helpdesk or Global Administrator.
  • App consents — the user (or an admin on their behalf) granted an application access — a classic phishing → persistence vector.
  • Password resets and MFA-method registration — the strong-authentication changes that so often follow an account takeover.
  • Conditional-Access edits and group changes that name the user.

A change appears on a person's timeline whether they made it (they were the actor) or were the subject of it (the target), so a single rail shows both “what did this admin do?” and “what was done to this account?”. Each card names the activity, the person who performed it, and what was affected; a failed change — for example an attempt to grant a privileged role that was denied — is ranked higher so it stands out. Clicking a card opens the full detail with a deep link to the Entra audit logs.

Like the rest of the timeline, this needs no new switch to turn on — it reuses the same audit permission the dashboard already requests. A tenant whose administrator has not yet approved that permission simply sees no teal cards; nothing else on the timeline is affected. The change history is also kept in a shared SharePoint list, so it remains readable across your admins and survives well beyond the few weeks Entra keeps the raw audit log.

Chapter 6The interactive map

A living map of where your tenant is being signed into — and where something looks wrong. Every sign-in plotted by location, arcs for travel that is physically impossible, a day/night terminator, and a 90-day window you can replay like a film.
Langate · Microsoft 365 Security
Interactive map

Interactive map

Two ways to look at the world

Flat map

The default. Countries are shaded by a metric you choose, cities show as bubbles, and impossible-travel arcs sweep between them. Scroll to zoom, drag to pan, or type a country name to fly straight to it.

Globe

Switch to Globe for a true 3-D planet you can grab and spin. Cities glow on the surface; spin round to see activity on the far side. Click any bubble to drill in.

Reading the colours

  • Country shading (the tint) — pick what it represents from the Tint dropdown: total sign-ins, failures, legacy-auth, or risky sign-ins. Darker = more.
  • City bubbles — one per location, sized by volume and coloured by health: green is clean, amber has failed sign-ins, and red has risky sign-ins. Red bubbles pulse so they catch your eye.
  • Arcs — an arc means one user appeared in two places too far apart, too fast — the classic shape of a stolen session or a logged-in attacker. A pulse travels along each arc; the colour rises with how impossible the jump is.
  • The dark overlay — the night side of the planet right now. A burst of sign-ins deep in the dark is worth a second look.

Use the layer buttons (Arcs, Cities, Day/Night, Grid) to turn any of these on or off, and the legend in the corner to remind yourself what each colour means.

Langate · Core Tenant Security
Interactive map · Digging in

Choosing a day — the time slider

Below the map sits a day slider covering the populated window (up to the last 90 days). Pick a day and the whole dashboard snaps to it: the From / To dates, the counts, and every tab scope to that day — so the numbers always match what you see. The map opens on the most recent day with sign-ins. To go back to the whole window, press Clear on the filter bar (or clear the date filter) and every day is back in view.

The slider sits over a small activity histogram — one bar per day, taller where there were more sign-ins, and tinted red for risky days, amber for days with failures, and green for clean ones — so you can aim straight for the busy or risky days instead of guessing. Each bar is clickable: click one to jump the whole dashboard to that day. As you drag the handle, a date bubble floats above it, and the two ends of the track are labelled (oldest day on the left, “Today” on the right).

Press ▶ Play to step through the days as a time-lapse. Playback drives the whole dashboard, not just the map — the From / To dates, the header counts, and whichever view you are on all advance day by day, so you can watch a week of activity unfold on any tab. The speed selector runs it at 1×, 2× or 4×, and Play resumes from wherever the handle is. You can also drive the slider from the keyboard: Space plays / pauses, the arrow keys nudge a day at a time, and Home / End jump to the oldest day or today.

Clicking a city or country

Click any city bubble (on the flat map or the globe) to open its detail panel:

  • A header with the country and the sign-in / failed / risky counts. (The city name is the panel's title, so it isn't repeated.)
  • A collapsible card per user who signed in from here. As soon as more than one person signed in from a city the cards start collapsed — click a name to expand it — and the panel scrolls so a busy city stays a sensible size. Each card, once open, shows the rich per-person detail described below.
  • Below the people, any impossible-travel legs that touch this city — the far city and the implied speed are shown on the line, with the distance on the hover tooltip. A busy home city can have hundreds; only the most extreme are listed (worst first), with a “+N more” line for the rest.

Inside a person's card

Expand any user's card — in the city panel or the matching country panel — and you get a compact history for that one person, scoped to exactly where you clicked.

Last 90 days at a glance

Interactive map · Inside a person's card

Devices — and sign-ins with no device

Each card rolls up the devices the person used: the operating system is stated once, and each browser carries a count rather than a separate line per build.

Some sign-ins carry no device information at all — background token refreshes, mail apps, and other non-interactive or legacy connections. Rather than label these a meaningless “Unknown device”, the card now shows what it does know: a cloud icon and the connection method plus the app it reached — for example “Mobile Apps and Desktop Clients · Office 365 Exchange Online”. That turns a dead end into a real clue about how the account is being used.

The country panel shows the same per-person cards as the city panel, topped with a 30-day activity sparkline and at-a-glance Users / Failed / Risky / Browser counts for the whole country.

Langate · Core Tenant Security
Interactive map · Acting on a travel alert

Acting on an impossible-travel arc

An arc tells you an account appeared in two places it could not have travelled between — but a line on a map is only useful if you can act on it. Every arc is now interactive, in three steps.

1 · Hover

Point at any arc and a small card shows who it is, the route, and how many times faster than a jet the jump implies. The arc lights up and the rest fade back so you can see it clearly.

2 · The legs list

Thin arcs overlap and are hard to click, so press Legs in the toolbar to open a ranked list of every impossible-travel leg, worst first. Hovering a row lights its arc on the map, and vice-versa.

3 · The inspector

Click an arc — or a row in the legs list — to open the inspector, a panel that slides in from the right with everything you need to make a call:

  • The person, with a risk badge and how impossible the trip was.
  • Both ends of the leg — city, local time, IP address, device, and sign-in client — side by side, with the implied speed spelled out.
  • Why it's flagged: tags for off-hours sign-ins, risk signals, legacy-auth clients, and whether the user is already trusted.
  • Any matching Defender incident, with a button to open it in the Microsoft Defender portal.

Then act, without leaving the map:

  • Force sign-out — revoke every session for the user (with a confirmation first). Use this when the trip looks like a real compromise.
  • Open Timeline — jump to the person's full activity timeline to see the wider picture.
  • Mark trusted — add the user to the whitelist when the "impossible" trip is really a known VPN or proxy.
  • Copy details — copy a tidy summary to paste into a ticket or chat.

Force sign-out and Mark trusted use the very same actions as the Risk panel, so an arc, a risky-user row, and the timeline all act on one consistent set of controls. Sign-out propagation can take up to about ten minutes.

Chapter 7Roadmap & next steps

The first release covers Microsoft Entra sign-in activity end-to-end. The roadmap captures the parallel data sources that would complement that picture — starting with the network layer.
Langate · Microsoft 365 Security
Roadmap
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Next Steps

Integrate Ubiquiti / UniFi telemetry Planned

Ubiquiti’s UniFi platform exposes several APIs that pair well with the Entra view. Where Entra answers "who signed in from where," UniFi answers "what device, on which switch port, behind which firewall rule." Together they close the gap between identity events and network events.

Which API to use

API Hosting What it’s good for
UniFi Site Manager Cloud
api.ui.com		 Cloud, API key Fleet inventory and health across many sites. Read-mostly. Light on per-client security telemetry. Easy to authenticate.
UniFi Network Controller
/proxy/network/api		 Local controller or UniFi OS device The data goldmine for this use case. Events, IDS/IPS alarms, historical sessions, DPI per client, firewall config. Officially undocumented but well-mapped by the community.
UniFi Protect UniFi OS device Cameras, motion events, doorbell. Adjacent to physical-security correlation but out of scope for v1.
UISP UISP server, token auth ISP / WISP equipment. Only relevant if Langate ever monitors customer-edge gear directly.

What we would surface in the dashboard

  • Identity × network correlation: when a risky Entra sign-in happens, show which UniFi client matched the source IP and what app categories it’s been using (from DPI).
  • IDS/IPS overlay on the globe: the existing globe view already plots Entra dots by country; UniFi stat/alarm hits can render alongside, in red.
  • Session-history join: UniFi stat/sessions gives a per-client byte-and-duration log — a natural anomaly signal for the baseline view.
  • Firewall-rule lineage: reading rest/firewallrule lets the doc generate an up-to-date diagram of egress and inter-VLAN policy without screenshotting the UniFi UI.
Core Tenant Security · Next Steps
Langate  ·  49
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Next Steps

Build plan

  1. Decide auth boundary — the controller API needs a session cookie from a local controller, so a small shared proxy (Azure Function or container) is likely needed to keep credentials out of the browser. Site Manager Cloud is the opposite: an API key works directly from the SPFx web part via a CORS-friendly fetch.
  2. Add a UniFiClient alongside GraphSignInClient in the SPFx project, mirroring the same retry / paging / chunking pattern already used for Graph.
  3. Hold UniFi credentials behind the shared proxy (or in a tenant-shared SharePoint list, like the dashboard’s other configuration) — never in the browser, one consistent secret-handling story.
  4. Add a new dashboard view ("Network") through the existing view dispatch — one ctor-reference line, no new boilerplate in the web part.
Why this is a "next step" and not v1: Entra alone already answers the most-asked questions, and Ubiquiti coverage is uneven across Langate customers. We add it when a customer with UniFi gear requests it, not speculatively.

Chapter 8Deployment & reference

Everything an admin needs to stand the dashboard up: how to add it to a page, the Graph permissions to approve once, what it creates in your tenant, a short troubleshooting list, and a glossary of the terms used in this book.
Langate · Microsoft 365 Security
Deployment & reference
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Deployment · Install

Adding it to a page

  1. Upload CTS_SPFX_<version>.sppkg to your tenant App Catalog and deploy it (one-time, per tenant).
  2. On any SharePoint page, edit → add the Core Tenant Security web part. No properties to configure.
  3. The first load runs a cold sync (a full 90-day Graph pull) behind a splash; later loads warm-load instantly from the browser cache.

Approve the permissions — once

The web part requests delegated Microsoft Graph scopes. An admin approves them a single time per tenant:

  1. Open SharePoint Admin Center.
  2. Go to Advanced → API access.
  3. Approve each pending Core Tenant Security request (table overleaf). Approvals propagate in a minute or two — refresh the page and every feature lights up.

The signed-in admin also needs the Security Reader Entra role for the Defender Incidents and Alerts tabs. Everything is delegated — the tool never holds an app secret or acts as anyone but the signed-in admin.

Core Tenant Security · Deployment

Langate · Core Tenant Security
Deployment · Permissions

Every permission, and why

Graph scope What it powers
AuditLog.Read.AllReading the Entra sign-in logs — the core data source for every view.
User.Read.All
Group.Read.All		The user and group pickers in the filter bar, and resolving a group’s members when you filter by group.
SecurityIncident.Read.All
SecurityAlert.Read.All		The Defender XDR Incidents and Alerts tabs.
User.RevokeSessions.AllForce sign-out — revoking a user’s sessions from the Risk panel or an impossible-travel arc.
IdentityRiskyUser.ReadWrite.AllConfirm compromised and Dismiss risk write-backs.
User.EnableDisableAccount.AllDisable account — blocking all future sign-ins for a user.

What it creates in your tenant

On first run the web part provisions three lists on the current site, each inheriting the site’s permissions so every dashboard admin shares them:

  • CTS Incidents — the Defender incident mirror + your triage.
  • CTS Trusted Users — the risk whitelist.
  • CTS Action Log — the append-only audit trail.

Sign-in data itself is never written to SharePoint — it lives only in the browser’s IndexedDB cache, swept on a 90-day rolling window.

Reference · Troubleshooting

If something looks empty

  • Risk badge reads "Risk 0". No Entra-flagged risky users in the window. On tenants below Entra ID P2 the risk fields are always blank — this is the expected steady state.
  • "Defender XDR is not licensed on this tenant". Graph returned 403 — usually the two Security scopes are still pending approval; otherwise the tenant genuinely lacks the licence. The tab fails soft and never blocks the rest of the dashboard.
  • A Sign-out / write-back error modal. The matching action scope (see the permissions table) hasn’t been approved yet. Approve it and refresh.
  • Only one user appears. The sign-in query is tenant-wide, so this means the tenant genuinely has one active signer — not a scoping bug.

Good to know

  • The dashboard auto-refreshes every 30 seconds (the ring by the title), pausing while the tab is in the background.
  • Load example data swaps in a rich synthetic tenant — ideal for a demo or for exploring a view before live data has synced.
  • Timestamps everywhere are shown in your browser’s local time.
Core Tenant Security · Reference
Langate  ·  55
Langate · Core Tenant Security
Reference · Glossary

Glossary

Attempt · Succeeded · Failed
The dashboard’s vocabulary. Attempts = Succeeded + Failed. "Risky" is separate — a sign-in can be Risky and Succeeded.
Risky sign-in
A sign-in Entra Identity Protection scored as elevated risk (medium/high) or flagged atRisk / confirmedCompromised. Populated only on Entra ID P2.
Impossible travel
The same account appearing in two places too far apart to have travelled between in the elapsed time — drawn as an arc on the globe.
Baseline
A user’s rolled-up "normal": usual countries, devices, apps and active hours. Anomaly tags on the Timeline are measured against it.
Password spray
One source trying a few common passwords across many accounts. A spray that then logs an account in is the strongest "breached now" signal.
Conditional Access (CA)
Entra policies that allow, block, or add requirements (e.g. MFA) to a sign-in. The Sankey view shows how many sign-ins each policy actually touched.
Legacy authentication
Older protocols (basic auth, authenticated SMTP) that can’t do MFA — the most-exploited door in a tenant; surfaced on the Legacy-auth radar.
Defender XDR — incident / alert
Microsoft’s cross-product detections. An incident groups related alerts. Mirrored into the Incidents and Alerts tabs for shared triage.
Warm load
A returning visit that paints instantly from the browser’s IndexedDB cache while a background sync refreshes — no splash screen.
Write-back
An action that changes state in Entra (confirm compromised, dismiss risk, disable account), not just in the dashboard. Every write-back is audited.
Core Tenant Security · Reference
